blocks.text: A traveller develops profuse watery 'rice-water' diarrhoea within hours of infection with Vibrio cholerae. The bacterial toxin does not damage the gut lining; it jams a single molecular switch in enterocytes in the 'on' position, so a signalling pathway that should be brief runs without stopping.

blocks.markdown: Cells detect extracellular signals through **receptors**. **Cell-surface receptors** bind hydrophilic ligands (peptide hormones, catecholamines, neurotransmitters) that cannot cross the membrane, and relay the message inside through **second messengers**. **Intracellular (nuclear) receptors** bind lipophilic ligands that do cross the membrane. The largest family of surface receptors is the **G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs)**, seven-transmembrane proteins that act through heterotrimeric **G proteins** (alpha, beta and gamma subunits).

**The GPCR activation cycle.** (1) In the resting state the G protein alpha subunit binds **GDP** and is associated with beta-gamma. (2) Ligand binding changes the receptor, which acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF): alpha releases GDP and takes up **GTP**. (3) Alpha-GTP separates from beta-gamma, and either piece regulates an effector enzyme or channel. (4) The alpha subunit has intrinsic **GTPase** activity; it hydrolyses GTP to GDP, which switches it off, and it re-associates with beta-gamma. The signal is thus self-limiting.

rows: IP3 releases Ca2+ from the ER; DAG with Ca2+ activates protein kinase C (PKC)
blocks.caption: Three major G protein pathways

blocks.markdown: **cAMP.** Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cyclic AMP. In the inactive state PKA is a tetramer of two regulatory and two catalytic subunits; cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, releasing active catalytic subunits that phosphorylate target proteins on serine and threonine residues (for example, glycogen metabolism enzymes in liver). cAMP is destroyed by **phosphodiesterase** to AMP, which ends the signal; caffeine inhibits phosphodiesterases and so prolongs cAMP signals.

**Calcium.** Cytosolic Ca2+ is kept very low (about 100 nM at rest) compared with the extracellular fluid (about 1-2 mM) and the ER lumen, so a small opening of a channel produces a large rise. In the Gq pathway, PLC-beta cleaves the membrane lipid **PIP2** into **IP3**, which diffuses and opens IP3 receptor channels on the ER, releasing Ca2+, and **DAG**, which stays in the membrane and, with Ca2+, activates PKC. Ca2+ binds **calmodulin**, which activates kinases such as CaM kinase. Ca2+ is removed by pumps (SERCA into the ER, plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPase) and exchangers.

blocks.title: Following a Gq pathway
blocks.prompt: Acetylcholine binds the M3 muscarinic receptor on a smooth muscle cell. Describe the sequence that raises cytosolic calcium.

steps.text: The receptor activates Gq: alpha exchanges GDP for GTP.
Gq-alpha activates PLC-beta, which cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG.
IP3 binds IP3 receptors in the ER membrane, releasing stored Ca2+ into the cytosol.
Ca2+ binds calmodulin to promote contraction, and Ca2+ with DAG activates PKC.

blocks.answer: Gq, PLC, IP3, ER Ca2+ release (and DAG activating PKC).

rows: Lipophilic: steroid hormones, thyroid hormone, vitamin D, retinoids
Ligand-receptor complex binds hormone response elements on DNA and changes transcription
GPCRs (beta-adrenergic), ion-channel receptors, receptor tyrosine kinases
Oestrogen, glucocorticoid and thyroid hormone receptors
blocks.caption: Surface versus nuclear receptors

blocks.title: Amplification (simplified model)
blocks.text: Signals are amplified at each step. In a simplified teaching model, if one activated receptor activates 10 G proteins and each activated G protein switches on one adenylyl cyclase that makes 100 cAMP molecules while active, one receptor yields about $10 \times 100 = 1000$ cAMP. Real numbers vary widely.

blocks.title: Locking the switch on
blocks.prompt: Cholera toxin chemically modifies Gs alpha so that it cannot hydrolyse GTP. Predict the effect in an enterocyte.

steps.text: Without GTPase activity Gs alpha stays active, so adenylyl cyclase keeps making cAMP.
High cAMP keeps PKA active, which opens chloride channels in the apical membrane.
Chloride and water secretion into the lumen causes massive watery diarrhoea.

blocks.answer: Persistently high cAMP leads to excess chloride and water secretion.

items: GPCR cycle: GDP-bound resting alpha, GEF activity of the receptor, GTP exchange, subunit separation, GTP hydrolysis resets the switch.
Gs raises cAMP and activates PKA; Gi lowers cAMP; Gq makes IP3 (Ca2+ release) and DAG (PKC).
Phosphodiesterase terminates cAMP; pumps terminate Ca2+ signals.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A second messenger is generated inside the cell in response to the first messenger (the ligand), and is not the ligand itself. Also, nuclear receptor signalling is slower because it works by changing gene transcription.

points: GPCRs activate G proteins by promoting GDP-GTP exchange; intrinsic GTPase activity of alpha ends the signal.
cAMP (via PKA) and Ca2+ (via IP3 from PLC, calmodulin and DAG-PKC) are the key second messengers, terminated by phosphodiesterase and by calcium pumps.
Lipophilic hormones act through intracellular receptors that regulate transcription over hours, unlike the faster surface receptor pathways.

questions.stem: Which event normally switches off an activated G protein alpha subunit?

options.text: Hydrolysis of bound GTP to GDP by the alpha subunit's own GTPase activity
Phosphorylation of GTP by PKA
Binding of a second ligand to the receptor
Degradation of cAMP by phosphodiesterase

questions.correctOptionText: Hydrolysis of bound GTP to GDP by the alpha subunit's own GTPase activity

distractorRationale.b: PKA does not phosphorylate GTP to switch off G proteins.
distractorRationale.c: Further ligand does not turn the alpha subunit off.
distractorRationale.d: Phosphodiesterase terminates cAMP, not the G protein itself.

questions.explanation: The alpha subunit hydrolyses GTP to GDP and re-associates with beta-gamma, which turns off the signal. Phosphodiesterase acts later in the pathway by removing cAMP.

questions.stem: What does an agonist-bound GPCR do to its G protein?

options.text: Acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor so alpha swaps GDP for GTP
Phosphorylates alpha on tyrosine residues
Hydrolyses GTP bound to alpha
Cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG

questions.correctOptionText: Acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor so alpha swaps GDP for GTP
questions.explanation: The ligand-bound receptor promotes release of GDP from alpha, and GTP, which is more abundant in the cytosol, binds in its place. This activates alpha and releases beta-gamma.

questions.stem: A beta-adrenergic agonist relaxes airway smooth muscle through a receptor coupled to Gs. Which sequence follows receptor activation?

options.text: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, cAMP rises, and PKA phosphorylates target proteins
Gs activates PLC, IP3 rises, and calcium is released from the ER
Gs inhibits adenylyl cyclase and cAMP falls
Gs binds DNA and changes transcription

questions.correctOptionText: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, cAMP rises, and PKA phosphorylates target proteins

distractorRationale.d: Gs is not a transcription factor.

questions.explanation: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase to produce cAMP, which activates PKA. The stimulatory G protein therefore increases cAMP rather than lowering it.

questions.stem: Which pathway correctly describes how Gq-coupled receptors raise cytosolic calcium?

options.text: PLC-beta cleaves PIP2 to IP3, which opens IP3 receptors on the ER to release Ca2+
Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP, which opens ER calcium channels directly
DAG diffuses to the ER and releases Ca2+
PKA phosphorylates PIP2 into IP3

questions.correctOptionText: PLC-beta cleaves PIP2 to IP3, which opens IP3 receptors on the ER to release Ca2+

distractorRationale.b: cAMP acts through PKA and not by opening ER calcium channels.
distractorRationale.c: DAG stays in the membrane and activates PKC.

questions.explanation: PLC-beta produces two messengers: soluble IP3, which releases Ca2+ from the ER, and membrane-bound DAG, which activates PKC with Ca2+.

questions.stem: Caffeine inhibits phosphodiesterase. What is the expected effect on a cAMP-mediated response to adrenaline in a cell?

options.text: cAMP persists longer, prolonging the response
cAMP is degraded faster, shortening the response
G protein GTPase activity is blocked
Adenylyl cyclase is inhibited

questions.correctOptionText: cAMP persists longer, prolonging the response

distractorRationale.c: That is the effect of cholera toxin, not caffeine.
distractorRationale.d: Caffeine does not inhibit adenylyl cyclase.

questions.explanation: Phosphodiesterase converts cAMP to AMP and so terminates the signal. When it is inhibited, cAMP levels remain elevated for longer.

questions.stem: In a simplified teaching model, one activated receptor activates 20 Gs proteins, and each active Gs switches on one adenylyl cyclase that produces 150 cAMP molecules. How many cAMP molecules result from one activated receptor?
questions.explanation: Amplification multiplies across steps: 20 x 150 = 3000 cAMP per receptor. This is a toy model that illustrates how second-messenger cascades amplify the signal.

questions.stem: Cortisol acts on a cell through a receptor that, after binding, regulates transcription. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Cortisol is lipophilic and crosses the membrane to bind an intracellular receptor that acts on DNA hormone response elements
Cortisol binds a surface GPCR and acts through cAMP
Cortisol cannot enter cells and acts only through IP3
Its response occurs within seconds because it needs no new protein

questions.correctOptionText: Cortisol is lipophilic and crosses the membrane to bind an intracellular receptor that acts on DNA hormone response elements

distractorRationale.c: Steroids are lipophilic and enter cells.

questions.explanation: Steroid hormones are lipophilic and cross the plasma membrane; the receptor complex binds hormone response elements and alters transcription, so effects appear over hours.

questions.stem: Explain how cAMP and calcium act as second messengers, including how each signal is generated and terminated.
markingGuide: cAMP made from ATP by adenylyl cyclase (Gs stimulates, Gi inhibits).
cAMP activates PKA by releasing catalytic subunits, which phosphorylate targets.
Ca2+ released from ER via IP3 produced by PLC-beta cleaving PIP2, with DAG activating PKC.
Ca2+ binds calmodulin and is removed by pumps (SERCA, plasma membrane ATPase) and exchangers.
questions.explanation: Each messenger needs generation, action and termination. Ca2+ is unusual in that it is stored in the ER and released rather than synthesised.

questions.stem: Describe the GPCR activation cycle and explain why cholera toxin, which modifies Gs alpha so it cannot hydrolyse GTP, causes watery diarrhoea.
markingGuide: Ligand binding makes the receptor act as a GEF: alpha swaps GDP for GTP.
Alpha-GTP and beta-gamma separate and regulate effectors.
Intrinsic GTPase hydrolyses GTP to GDP and resets the switch.
Toxin prevents GTP hydrolysis so Gs stays active and cAMP stays high.
High cAMP/PKA opens chloride channels and drives water secretion, causing diarrhoea.
questions.explanation: Termination by GTP hydrolysis is the key point. Without it adenylyl cyclase remains stimulated and the enterocyte secretes chloride and water continuously.

questions.stem: Compare cell-surface receptors with intracellular nuclear receptors in terms of ligand properties, location, mechanism, and speed of response, giving an example of each.
markingGuide: Surface receptors bind hydrophilic ligands that cannot cross the membrane; examples beta-adrenergic receptor.
They use second messengers or kinase cascades; response in seconds to minutes.
Nuclear receptors bind lipophilic ligands that cross the membrane; example oestrogen or glucocorticoid receptor.
The ligand-receptor complex binds hormone response elements and alters transcription.
Nuclear receptor responses take hours because new protein must be made.
questions.explanation: The lipophilicity of the ligand determines where its receptor must be and thereby the mechanism and speed.
